A care manager has hundreds of visit notes and forms. Here, three hundred and thirty six visits, and twenty three forms. They want to ask a plain question, and get an answer they can check. In about ten minutes, four parts. How one question becomes a checked answer. What limits keep it safe, and why. What is checked, and what is fragile. And what breaks first as it grows, and how to fix it.

Part one. One question, end to end. There are four places: the page, the server, the model, and the database. The manager types: are there any medication issues I should know about? The page sends the question to the server, with the last six messages as history. Enough for a follow-up like, and what about Alfred, without re-sending the whole conversation.

The server gives the request an I D. Every log line for this question carries it, so a bad answer can be traced. Then the agent builds the prompt. Instructions. The schema, read from the live database. The list of people. And a glossary of what the data cannot show. The schema and the people are read from the data, so they cannot go stale. The glossary is the one hand-written part, so it is the part that can. All of it is the same for every question, so the provider caches it. Only the question is new.

The model has one tool: run SQL. No search tool, and no report tools. It writes the query itself, reads the rows, and decides whether to ask again. When a turn has no query, that turn is the answer. Nothing checks that it is complete. The prompt tells it to read a person's notes before calling them fine, and to say what it could not determine.

The database runs the query read only. Every row it returns carries the I D of the record it came from. This row says the family did not give the morning medication, again. It is visit two ninety three.
The model writes the answer, and puts that I D right after the sentence it supports. The I D has travelled from the database row into the text.

The answer streams back to the page as lines of JSON. The page looks for one pattern: the word visit or form, then a number, in brackets. Each match becomes a button. Tap it, and the page fetches that exact record, and shows it next to the sentence. The manager checks the claim against the source, in one tap.
Part two. The limits, and what happens when each one trips. The rule is simple. Every limit fails loudly, and hands the problem back to the model, not to the manager.

Each query gets two seconds, so one bad query cannot hang the question. Too slow, and the model is told to narrow it. Each result keeps two hundred rows, five hundred characters a cell, and thirty thousand characters in all. Why? Two hundred rows of long notes is about twenty five thousand tokens in one step. The caps keep each step cheap, and small enough for the model to read carefully. Cut short, and the result says truncated, so the model asks a smaller question.

Each question gets eight tool steps, a hundred and fifty thousand prompt tokens, and two minutes. A normal question needs a few steps and about fifteen seconds. The bounds are there so one confused question cannot spend without limit. Whichever trips first, the next turn has no tools. The model must answer with what it found, and say what it could not determine. That closing section is a rule in the prompt. The glossary tells the model what the data cannot show, like planned visit times, and the page draws the section as its own box. Nothing checks it is right. It is the model's judgement, with the glossary as its guide.

Eight questions can run at once. Each one costs model tokens and holds a server thread, so this caps the spend and keeps the server responsive. The ninth is told it is busy, and to try again. And the database is opened read only, twice over. The model writes its own SQL, so the database itself must refuse writes, not just the prompt. Ask it to change a record, and it says it is read only, and stops.

Part three. What is checked, and what is fragile. Checked: a test keeps the page and the prompt agreeing on the citation format. Evals fail any answer that cites a record that does not exist. Forty two of forty two passed on the app's model. And a citation in the wrong format stays plain text, so the mistake is visible. Not checked: whether the record really supports the sentence. A real I D on the wrong record looks exactly like a right one. That is still the manager's call, and it is why the record is one tap away.
Part four. What breaks first, in order, and the fix for each, in plain words.

One: recall. Recall means: of the people who need attention, how many did the agent find. Today it finds all five. But in this data, the warnings repeat the same few phrases, so they are easy to spot. Real carers write the same thing a hundred ways. If the agent misses someone, nothing errors. The answer just looks complete. That is why it comes first: it fails silently. The first fix is to measure it, with real notes and real managers. The structural fix is to shortlist people with SQL, read each person's notes in a small context of their own, in parallel, then rank them. A model reading one person carefully misses less than a model reading everyone at once.

Two: the database as it grows. The raw data keeps each visit's activities as nested JSON. So the app builds a read model: views that flatten every note, comment and form answer into one row each, plus a full text search index. Today that is rebuilt on every connection, which takes about six milliseconds. And a search like, comment contains medication, cannot use an index, so it reads every row. Both grow with the data. On a big database, queries slow down until they hit the two second limit, and the model is told to narrow, again and again. The fix: build the read model once and store it, keep the search index updated by triggers when data changes, and add real indexes on person and date. On Postgres, a read-only role and a statement timeout replace today's guards.

Three: many people at once. Each live question holds one server thread for its whole run, up to two minutes, and most of that time the thread is just waiting for the model. So the server allows eight at a time, and turns the ninth away as busy. That is honest back pressure: refuse early, rather than let everyone slow down. The fix has two parts. Async model calls, so a waiting question holds no thread, and thousands can wait cheaply. Then a queue with a quota per user, so when the model provider is the bottleneck, people wait in line, and one heavy user cannot crowd out the rest. Quotas need sign-in first.

Also missing today: durability. A question lives only inside its open connection. Close the page, or restart the server, and the answer is gone. Every query only reads, so asking again is always safe. It is just paid for twice. The durable version stores each question as a job, with a key from the page, so a retry never runs twice. Workers run the job and append its events to a log, the same lines of JSON the page reads today, so the page can reconnect and carry on where it left off.

Four: the long conversation. Every step re-sends the whole conversation: the prompt, and every query and result so far. So each step costs more than the last, and models read the middle of a long context less carefully. The per-person fan out from fix one solves this too: many small contexts instead of one big one. And five, the gate before any real use. Today there is no sign-in, and any record can be fetched by its I D. Real use needs sign-in, and every lookup scoped to the caller's organisation, so one care company can never see another's records.
So, in one breath. One generic tool, over a schema read from the data. Hard limits that hand problems back to the model. And every claim, one tap from its source.
